         se        = round(as.numeric(SE(boot)), 3)) %>%
    mutate(ci_low   = indirect - 1.96 * se,
           ci_high  = indirect + 1.96 * se,
           mediated = ifelse(ci_low > 0 | ci_high < 0, "yes", "no"),
           `95% CI` = paste0("[", round(ci_low, 3), ", ", round(ci_high, 3), "]"),
           `% of total` = ifelse(mediated == "yes",
                                 paste0(round(100 * indirect / total), "%"), "")) %>%
    dplyr::select(predictor, total, direct, indirect, se, `95% CI`,
                  mediated, `% of total`)
}

set.seed(42)
med_hunt <- indirect_tbl("hunting_support")
med_trap <- indirect_tbl("trapping_support")

med_hunt %>% ktab(caption = "Indirect effects through identity: hunting support")
med_trap %>% ktab(caption = "Indirect effects through identity: trapping support")

apaths <- map_dfr(blocks$identity, function(m) {
  fit <- svyglm(build_formula(m, c(blocks$demographics, blocks$exposure,
                                   antecedent_terms)), design = design_cc)
  tidy_svyglm(fit) %>%
    filter(term %in% value_terms) %>%
    mutate(mediator = m)
})

apaths %>%
  mutate(b = paste0(round(estimate, 3), stars(p))) %>%
  dplyr::select(mediator, term, b, se) %>%
  ktab(caption = "a-paths: values predicting the identity composites")

# The two identity composites share a dominant general factor (omega_h = .77,
# r = .58), so a predictor of one shows a weak association with the other purely
# through shared variance. Re-estimating the non-consumptive a-paths with
# consumptive identity controlled isolates the specific component.
apaths_ctrl <- svyglm(
  build_formula("ID_non_consume_z",
                c("ID_consum_z", antecedent_terms, blocks$demographics,
                  blocks$exposure)),
  design = design_cc)

tidy_svyglm(apaths_ctrl) %>%
  filter(term %in% antecedent_terms) %>%
  mutate(b = paste0(round(estimate, 3), stars(p))) %>%
  dplyr::select(term, b, se) %>%
  ktab(caption = paste("Non-consumptive identity with consumptive identity",
                       "controlled: the specific component, net of the general",
                       "identification factor."))

ap_ctrl <- function(term) {
  fmt(tidy_svyglm(apaths_ctrl)$estimate[tidy_svyglm(apaths_ctrl)$term == term], 3)
}

# Evidence that the four antecedents are empirically distinct rather than one
# underlying dimension: how strongly they intercorrelate, and their VIFs in the
# full model.
ant_cor   <- cor(model_cc[, antecedent_terms], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
ant_max_r <- max(abs(ant_cor[lower.tri(ant_cor)]))
ant_vif   <- vif_tbl %>%
  filter(term %in% antecedent_terms) %>%
  pull(`VIF equivalent`)

# accessors for the prose
med_get <- function(tbl, pred, col) {
  v <- tbl[[col]][tbl$predictor == pred]
  if (is.numeric(v)) sprintf("%.3f", v) else as.character(v)
}
a_get <- function(mediator, term) {
  sprintf("%.3f", apaths$estimate[apaths$mediator == mediator & apaths$term == term])
}
```

```{r results path model, echo=F, include=T, warning=F, message=F, fig.height=4.8, fig.width=9, fig.alt="Path diagram of significant effects. Domination and Christian nationalism have arrows to consumptive identity; mutualism and political ideology have arrows to non-consumptive identity. Only consumptive identity has an arrow to support. Direct paths from mutualism, domination and political ideology to support are also shown. Christian nationalism has no significant direct path."}
# Results figure is built from the fitted coefficients, not drawn by hand, so it
# cannot disagree with the tables.
results_edges <- function(dv, model, alpha = 0.05) {
  a <- apaths %>%
    filter(p < alpha) %>%
    transmute(from = term, to = mediator, kind = "a",
              est = estimate, lab = fmt(estimate, 2))

  m <- tidy_svyglm(model) %>% filter(p < alpha)

  b <- m %>%
    filter(term %in% blocks$identity) %>%
    transmute(from = term, to = "outcome", kind = "b",
              est = estimate, lab = fmt(estimate, 2))

  d <- m %>%
    filter(term %in% antecedent_terms) %>%
    transmute(from = term, to = "outcome", kind = "direct",
              est = estimate, lab = fmt(estimate, 2))

  bind_rows(a, b, d) %>%
    left_join(node_xy, by = c("from" = "node")) %>%
    left_join(node_xy, by = c("to" = "node"), suffix = c("", "end"))
}

res_plots <- map2(c("hunting_support", "trapping_support"),
                  list(hunt_lin, trap_lin),
                  function(dv, m) {
                    # name the outcome node rather than relying on a panel title
                    out_lab <- if (dv == "hunting_support") "Hunting\nsupport"
                               else "Trapping\nsupport"
                    nd <- nodes %>%
                      mutate(label = ifelse(node == "outcome", out_lab, label))
                    path_plot(results_edges(dv, m), nd, show_labels = TRUE,
                              split_curves = TRUE)
                  })

results_plot <- patchwork::wrap_plots(res_plots, ncol = 2) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(
    caption = wrap_cap(c("Significant paths only (p < .05), design-weighted.",
                         "All values are unstandardized coefficients. Black straight",
                         "arrows are paths through identity; grey curved arrows are direct",
                         "paths from the antecedent orientations to support. Absence of an",
                         "arrow indicates a non-significant path."), width = 110),
    theme = theme(plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey45", hjust = 0,
                                              size = rel(0.8), family = fam)))

results_plot

ggsave(here("figs", "path_model_results.png"), results_plot,
       width = 9, height = 4.8, dpi = 300, device = agg_png)
```

A note on reading the *a*-paths. Christian nationalism shows a weak positive path to non-consumptive identity (`r a_get("ID_non_consume_z", "christian_nationalism_score_z")`) alongside its much stronger path to consumptive identity. That crossover is an artifact of the general factor rather than a substantive association: the two composites correlate .58 and share a dominant general dimension, so any predictor of one shows a weak association with the other through shared variance alone. Estimating the same paths with consumptive identity controlled, isolating the specific component, reverses the sign to `r ap_ctrl("christian_nationalism_score_z")`, and domination moves from null to `r ap_ctrl("wvo_domination_z")`. Net of general identification the structure is cleanly bipolar: mutualism (`r ap_ctrl("wvo_mutualism_z")`) and political ideology (`r ap_ctrl("political_ideology_z")`) push toward non-consumptive identification, domination and Christian nationalism away from it. The uncontrolled paths are reported above because they are the ones the mediation model uses; the controlled estimates are the ones to interpret substantively.

The two panels make the central result visible. Every orientation reaches support somehow, but they take different routes. Mutualism, domination and political ideology retain direct paths after identity is controlled. Christian nationalism does not reach trapping support directly at all, and reaches hunting support only weakly. For both outcomes its main route runs through consumptive identity. And of the two identity constructs, only the consumptive one carries a path forward.

## Interpretation

The findings below are ordered by how much they change the picture, not by effect size. The full models account for `r pc_of(hunt_lin)`% of the variance in hunting support and `r pc_of(trap_lin)`% in trapping support.

**The four antecedent orientations are independent of one another and reach support by different routes.** This is the central result, and it cuts against a common simplification. Wildlife value orientations, political ideology and Christian nationalism are routinely treated, in commentary and often implicitly in interpretation, as facets of a single conservative-versus-liberal disposition toward wildlife. They are not.

They are empirically distinct to begin with. The largest correlation among the four is `r fmt(ant_max_r)`, their variance inflation factors range from `r fmt(min(ant_vif))` to `r fmt(max(ant_vif))`, and all four retain effects in the presence of the other three. The two blocks contribute comparably to explained variance: ideological orientations add `r d_r2(hunt_models, "ideological")` and wildlife value orientations `r d_r2(hunt_models, "wvo")` for hunting support, `r d_r2(trap_models, "ideological")` and `r d_r2(trap_models, "wvo")` for trapping. Neither family is redundant with the other.

More importantly, they behave differently. Each predicts one identity and not the other: domination and Christian nationalism predict consumptive identity, with mutualism and political ideology null; mutualism and political ideology predict non-consumptive identity, with domination null. Net of the general identification factor the separation is sharper still, with domination and Christian nationalism predicting non-consumptive identity *negatively*. And each takes a different route to the outcome: one fully through identity, one partly, two not at all. Four predictors a reader might expect to be near-substitutes operate through four distinguishable mechanisms.

**Christian nationalism reaches support almost entirely through identity.** For trapping support its direct effect is `r med_get(med_trap, "christian_nationalism_score_z", "direct")` and not significant, while its indirect effect through consumptive identity is `r med_get(med_trap, "christian_nationalism_score_z", "indirect")` with a bootstrap interval of `r med_get(med_trap, "christian_nationalism_score_z", "95% CI")`, or `r med_get(med_trap, "christian_nationalism_score_z", "% of total")` of the total effect. For hunting support the indirect route accounts for `r med_get(med_hunt, "christian_nationalism_score_z", "% of total")`, alongside a small direct effect that remains significant.

The substantive reading is that Christian nationalism does not generate beliefs about wildlife. Were it doing so, it would show a direct path in the way mutualism does. What it appears to track is membership in a particular social and moral world, and that membership predicts support. The wildlife attitude is downstream of social location rather than of theology. Domination sits between the two cases, working partly through identity (`r med_get(med_hunt, "wvo_domination_z", "% of total")` of its total effect for hunting, `r med_get(med_trap, "wvo_domination_z", "% of total")` for trapping) and partly directly, which fits a construct that is both a belief about human–animal relations and a stance associated with particular communities.

**Identity is an asymmetric pathway.** Consumptive identity is the strongest of the constructs of theoretical interest (`r b_of(hunt_lin, "ID_consum_z")` for hunting, `r b_of(trap_lin, "ID_consum_z")` for trapping), exceeding any single value orientation. Non-consumptive identity predicts neither outcome (`r b_of(hunt_lin, "ID_non_consume_z")`, `r b_of(trap_lin, "ID_non_consume_z")`).

That null is a result rather than a failure, and it is more interesting than it first appears. Non-consumptive identity is a reliable, well-structured construct with coherent antecedents: mutualism (`r a_get("ID_non_consume_z", "wvo_mutualism_z")`) and political ideology (`r a_get("ID_non_consume_z", "political_ideology_z")`) both predict it strongly. The pathway into it exists and then dead-ends. Mutualism and political ideology shape identity; they simply shape an identity that does not carry forward to positions on these practices. Identifying with hunters, ranchers and landowners commits a person to something; identifying with environmentalists, wildlife viewers and outdoor recreationists does not, at least not here.

**The two identities are not opposing poles.** They correlate positively, and a general factor accounts for most of the reliable variance across the nine items. People who identify with consumptive groups also tend to identify with non-consumptive ones. A literature treating these as a trade-off is assuming a structure the data contradict, and the asymmetry above means the two are not merely non-opposed but differently consequential.

**Social exposure matters more for hunting than for trapping.** Knowing a hunter predicts support for both practices, but the effect is well over twice as large for hunting (`r b_of(hunt_lin, "knows_hunter")`) as for trapping (`r b_of(trap_lin, "knows_hunter")`), and the hierarchical decomposition is starker still: exposure adds `r d_r2(hunt_models, "exposure")` to R² for hunting against `r d_r2(trap_models, "exposure")` for trapping. Personal familiarity normalizes hunting substantially and trapping only marginally, which is what one would expect if acquaintance conveys information about hunting specifically rather than about consumptive wildlife use in general. The cut-point analysis sharpens this further: the effect concentrates at the bottom of the scale, moving people out of outright opposition without pushing them toward strong support.

**Wildlife value orientations behave as the cognitive hierarchy predicts.** Mutualism is negatively associated with support for both practices (`r b_of(hunt_lin, "wvo_mutualism_z")`, `r b_of(trap_lin, "wvo_mutualism_z")`) and domination positively (`r b_of(hunt_lin, "wvo_domination_z")`, `r b_of(trap_lin, "wvo_domination_z")`), all at *p* < .001, and both retain their effects after identity is entered. Political ideology contributes independently but more modestly (`r b_of(hunt_lin, "political_ideology_z")`, `r b_of(trap_lin, "political_ideology_z")`).

**Several demographic effects are substantial.** Women are less supportive of both practices (`r b_of(hunt_lin, "female")`, `r b_of(trap_lin, "female")`). Dietary position matters for hunting in particular: respondents who eat meat are `r b_of(hunt_lin, "eats_meat_n")` scale points more supportive of hunting than those who do not, though the vegetarian group is small (about 6%) and the estimate correspondingly imprecise. Age is associated with lower support for both, and markedly so for trapping (`r b_of(trap_lin, "age_group50-64")` and `r b_of(trap_lin, "age_group65+")`, against `r b_of(hunt_lin, "age_group50-64")` and `r b_of(hunt_lin, "age_group65+")` for hunting). Middle-income respondents are more supportive than the lowest bracket, though the pattern is not monotonic. Education and pet ownership are unrelated to either outcome.

**The two outcomes differ in what drives them.** Hunting support is more responsive to personal experience (knowing a hunter, eating meat), while trapping support is more strongly patterned by age, with respondents over 50 markedly less supportive. Christian nationalism's route to trapping is almost wholly indirect, where for hunting a direct path remains. Trapping appears to be the more socially distant practice: fewer people have direct experience of it, and attitudes toward it are correspondingly more a function of who someone is than of what they have encountered.

## Robustness: is consumptive identity distinct from support?

The consumptive identity scale includes `identify_hunters`, and it is reasonable to ask whether identifying with hunters is meaningfully different from supporting hunting. If the identity effect were a restatement of the outcome, the analysis would be circular.

```{r identity distinctness, echo=F, include=T, warning=F, message=F}
consum_items    <- identity_scales$ID_consum
consum_items_nh <- setdiff(consum_items, "identify_hunters")

# use = "complete.obs": identity ITEMS can be missing where the composite is
# not, because the min-items rule tolerates gaps. Without it cor() returns NA.
r_with <- function(x, y) cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs")

tibble(measure = c("Consumptive identity (6 items)",
                   "Consumptive identity (excluding identify_hunters)",
                   "identify_hunters (single item)"),
       `r with hunting support`  = c(
         r_with(model_cc$ID_consum,        model_cc$hunting_support),
         r_with(composite(model_cc, consum_items_nh), model_cc$hunting_support),
         r_with(model_cc$identify_hunters, model_cc$hunting_support)),
       `r with trapping support` = c(
         r_with(model_cc$ID_consum,        model_cc$trapping_support),
         r_with(composite(model_cc, consum_items_nh), model_cc$trapping_support),
         r_with(model_cc$identify_hunters, model_cc$trapping_support))) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) %>%
  ktab(caption = "Association between consumptive identity and the outcomes")

# refit both outcomes with the reduced composite
model_cc <- model_cc %>%
  mutate(ID_consum_nh_z = as.numeric(scale(composite(., consum_items_nh))))
design_nh <- model_cc %>% as_survey_design(ids = 1, weights = weight)

preds_nh <- gsub("^ID_consum_z$", "ID_consum_nh_z", all_predictors)

nh_fits <- map(outcome_vars, ~ svyglm(build_formula(.x, preds_nh),
                                      design = design_nh)) %>%
  setNames(outcome_vars)

map_dfr(outcome_vars, function(dv) {
  full <- if (dv == "hunting_support") hunt_lin else trap_lin
  tibble(Outcome = dv,
         `b (6 items)`   = fmt(coef(full)[["ID_consum_z"]], 3),
         `b (5 items)`   = fmt(coef(nh_fits[[dv]])[["ID_consum_nh_z"]], 3),
         `R2 (6 items)`  = fmt(r2_svyglm(full), 3),
         `R2 (5 items)`  = fmt(r2_svyglm(nh_fits[[dv]]), 3))
}) %>%
  ktab(caption = paste("Consumptive identity effect with and without the",
                       "hunting item. Both reduced-model coefficients remain",
                       "significant at p < .001."))
```

Three observations argue that the constructs are distinct. The composite correlates `r fmt(r_with(model_cc$ID_consum, model_cc$hunting_support))` with hunting support, sharing roughly `r fmt(100 * r_with(model_cc$ID_consum, model_cc$hunting_support)^2, 0)`% of its variance, related but far from redundant. The single most exposed item, `identify_hunters`, correlates `r fmt(r_with(model_cc$identify_hunters, model_cc$hunting_support))` with hunting support and `r fmt(r_with(model_cc$identify_hunters, model_cc$trapping_support))` with trapping support; a proxy for hunting attitudes would not track trapping almost equally well. And removing that item leaves the identity effect significant in both models with R² changing by less than .01, and leaves every mediation result intact.

The six-item composite is retained. Dropping a cleanly loading item to pre-empt an objection would concede more than the evidence warrants, though the reduced specification is available as a robustness check.

term_labels <- c(
  "age_group30-49"                = "Age 30-49",
  "age_group50-64"                = "Age 50-64",
  "age_group65+"                  = "Age 65+",
  "income_cat15-50k"              = "Income 15-50k",
  "income_cat50-75k"              = "Income 50-75k",
  "income_cat75-100k"             = "Income 75-100k",
  "income_cat100-150k"            = "Income 100-150k",
  "income_cat150-200k"            = "Income 150-200k",
  "income_cat200k+"               = "Income 200k+",
  "female"                        = "Female",
  "college_grad"                  = "College graduate",
  "has_pets_n"                    = "Has pets",
  "eats_meat_n"                   = "Eats meat",
  "knows_hunter"                  = "Knows a hunter",
  "wvo_mutualism_z"               = "Mutualism",
  "wvo_domination_z"              = "Domination",

block_labels <- c(demographics   = "Demographics",
                  exposure       = "Exposure",
                  ideological = "Ideological orientations",
                  wvo            = "Wildlife value orientations",
                  identity       = "Identity")

assign_block <- function(terms) {
  map_chr(terms, function(tm) {
    hit <- map_lgl(blocks, ~ any(str_starts(tm, fixed(.x))))
    if (any(hit)) names(blocks)[which(hit)[1]] else NA_character_
  })
}

tidy_full <- function(m, outcome) {
  tidy_svyglm(m) %>%
    mutate(outcome   = outcome,
           conf_low  = estimate - qnorm(0.975) * se,
           conf_high = estimate + qnorm(0.975) * se,
           block     = assign_block(term),
           label     = coalesce(term_labels[term], term))
}

coefs <- bind_rows(tidy_full(hunt_lin, "Hunting support"),
                   tidy_full(trap_lin, "Trapping support")) %>%
  mutate(block   = factor(block, levels = names(block_labels), labels = block_labels),
         outcome = factor(outcome, levels = c("Hunting support", "Trapping support")))

# a term failing to match a block would vanish from the figure without warning
stopifnot(!any(is.na(coefs$block)))
```

```{r figure coefficients, echo=F, include=T, warning=F, message=F, fig.height=6, fig.width=8}
plot_order <- coefs %>%
  filter(outcome == "Hunting support") %>%
  arrange(block, estimate) %>%
  pull(label)

coef_plot <- coefs %>%
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = plot_order)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = label, color = block, shape = block)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf_low, xmax = conf_high), height = 0, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ outcome) +
  # sized from the number of blocks, so adding or splitting a block cannot
  # leave the palette short
  scale_color_manual(values = okabe_ito[seq_along(block_labels)]) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 17, 15, 18, 8)[seq_along(block_labels)]) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(x = "Change in support (scale points)", y = NULL,
       caption = wrap_cap(paste0(
         "Design-weighted linear regression, n = ", n_fmt(nrow(model_cc)),
         ". Points are coefficients with 95% confidence intervals. Continuous ",
         "predictors are standardized, so estimates are scale points per SD. ",
         "Reference categories: age 18-29, income under 15k."), width = 105)) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor   = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey92", linewidth = 0.3),
        legend.title    = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top",
        plot.caption    = element_text(color = "grey45", hjust = 0, size = rel(0.75)),
        axis.title      = element_text(color = "grey20"),
        strip.text      = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))

coef_plot

ggsave(here("figs", "coefficient_plot.png"), coef_plot,
       width = 8, height = 6, dpi = 300, device = agg_png)
```

```{r table 1 sample, echo=F, include=T, warning=F, message=F}
cat_summary <- map_dfr(c("age_group", "income_cat"), function(v) {
  unwt <- model_cc %>% count(level = .data[[v]]) %>%
    mutate(variable = v, pct_unwt = 100 * n / sum(n))
  wt <- design_cc %>% group_by(level = !!sym(v)) %>%
    dplyr::summarize(pct_wt = survey_prop(vartype = NULL)) %>%
    mutate(pct_wt = 100 * pct_wt)
  left_join(unwt, wt, by = "level")
})

bin_summary <- map_dfr(c("female", "college_grad", "has_pets_n", "eats_meat_n",
                         "knows_hunter"), function(v) {
  tibble(variable = v, level = "Yes",
         n        = sum(model_cc[[v]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
         pct_unwt = 100 * mean(model_cc[[v]], na.rm = TRUE),
         pct_wt   = 100 * as.numeric(coef(svymean(make.formula(v), design_cc,
                                                  na.rm = TRUE))))
})

bind_rows(cat_summary, bin_summary) %>%
  mutate(variable = coalesce(term_labels[variable], variable),
         across(c(pct_unwt, pct_wt), ~ round(.x, 1))) %>%
  dplyr::select(Variable = variable, Level = level, n,
                `% unweighted` = pct_unwt, `% weighted` = pct_wt) %>%
  ktab(caption = paste0("Table 1. Sample characteristics (n = ", n_fmt(nrow(model_cc)),
                        "). Percentages unweighted and design-weighted."))
```

```{r table 2 correlations, echo=F, include=T, warning=F, message=F}
cont_raw <- c("hunting_support", "trapping_support", "wvo_mutualism",
              "wvo_domination", "political_ideology",
              "christian_nationalism_score", "ID_consum", "ID_non_consume")

cont_labels <- c("Hunting support", "Trapping support", "Mutualism", "Domination",
                 "Political ideology", "Christian nationalism",
                 "Consumptive identity", "Non-consumptive identity")

cor_mat <- cor(model_cc[, cont_raw], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_mat[upper.tri(cor_mat, diag = TRUE)] <- NA

tibble(Variable = paste0(seq_along(cont_raw), ". ", cont_labels),
       Mean     = round(colMeans(model_cc[, cont_raw], na.rm = TRUE), 2),
       SD       = round(apply(model_cc[, cont_raw], 2, sd, na.rm = TRUE), 2)) %>%
  bind_cols(as.data.frame(round(cor_mat, 2)) %>% setNames(seq_along(cont_raw))) %>%
  ktab(caption = paste("Table 2. Descriptives and correlations among continuous",
                       "variables, on original response scales. Correlations",
                       "are unweighted."))
```

```{r table 3 full model, echo=F, include=T, warning=F, message=F}
coef_wide <- coefs %>%
  mutate(cell = paste0(sprintf("%.3f", estimate), stars(p),
                       " (", sprintf("%.3f", se), ")")) %>%
  dplyr::select(block, label, outcome, cell) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = cell) %>%
  arrange(block)

block_index <- coef_wide %>% count(block) %>% deframe()

coef_wide %>%
  dplyr::select(Predictor = label, `Hunting support`, `Trapping support`) %>%
  kable(caption = paste0(
    "Table 3. Design-weighted linear regression predicting support for hunting ",
    "and trapping (n = ", n_fmt(nrow(model_cc)), "). Cells are unstandardized ",
    "coefficients with standard errors in parentheses. Continuous predictors ",
    "are standardized. Reference categories: age 18-29, income under 15k. ",
    "* p < .05, ** p < .01, *** p < .001.")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"),
                full_width = FALSE, position = "left") %>%
  pack_rows(index = block_index)
```

Table 3 and the coefficient figure carry the same information deliberately. Most journals will take one or the other; the figure communicates the pattern at a glance, the table gives exact values. Whichever does not appear in the main text works as a supplement.
